newsitem.title: UK: Markets to focus on dollar-yen and FOMC meeting.
newsitem.headline: Markets to focus on dollar-yen and FOMC meeting.

text.p: A meeting of the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) and Japanese September trade and current account data will be the main highlights for financial markets in the coming week, analysts said on Friday.
While Wednesday's meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve's rate-setting FOMC is expected to bring no change in interest rate policy, it will still exert an influence on the markets.

"The economic slowdown and continued good behaviour of inflation mean people are going to be fairly relaxed (about interest rates)," said Ian Harwood, head of strategy and economics at Kleinwort Benson in London.
He said there would still be some residual anxiety that the Fed may raise rates, but it was most unlikely to happen.

U.S. October producer price and consumer price data, on Wednesday and Thursday respectively, will affect bond market sentiment if they come in higher than expected, but forecasts were muted, analysts said.
Harwood said Thursday's October retail sales and Friday's industrial production were also likely to show continued easing of economic growth.

In Japan, markets will be looking for comments and indications about dollar/yen after comments from Japanese Ministry of Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara on Thursday that the dollar's recovery was about to end.
"The Japanese current account figures will be influential there," said Paul Donovan, senior economist at UBS in London.
The September trade balance and current account data, to be published Monday, are expected to justify the shift in policy and indicate a stronger yen policy in the future.
"The weak yen policy has been very useful in stimulating the Japanese economy but has outlived its usefulness," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
He said the pace of decline in the trade surplus was slowing and players would scrutinise the data for signs of confidence that trade trends were changing.

Harwood said trade account data would be watched for a strong revival in exports and a deceleration of import growth. "The trade figures might not be as conducive to good relations between the U.S. and Japan as people have been assuming."
It will be a busy week in Britain. October producer prices, due on Monday, are forecast to show a rise in output of 0.2 percent compared with a rise of 0.4 in September.
"On Wednesday there is another welter of inflation data with average earnings and unemployment," said Harwood.
October retail prices on Thursday will also be key.

"There is growing concern that above-trend economic growth is jeopardising inflation stability and the market will be sensitive to any indications that inflation is now in an upward trend," said Meggyesi.
In Europe, markets will watch Thursday's meeting of the Bank of France.
"The French economy still needs all the help it can get from lower interest rates, particularly as French banks aren't passing on the full benefits of cheaper money," said Harwood.
"People will probably be looking for a further cut in rates at some point."

Meggyesi said the focus for investors in Italian markets will be November 17's deadline for the lower house of parliament to approve the 1997 budget, after which markets will be hoping for a cut in interest rates and a decision about re-entry to the ERM.
